items.line: I find myself regrettably unable to accede to your request.
items.right: No.
wrong: Yes, gladly.
I did not hear you.
Ask me tomorrow.
items.why: To accede is to agree. Unable to agree is just a polite no.

items.line: My stomach has commenced a formal protest against the prolonged absence of lunch.
items.right: I am very hungry.
wrong: I feel sick.
I ate too much at lunch.
Lunch has been moved to noon.
items.why: To commence is to begin, and prolonged means long: a stomach protesting no lunch is hungry.

items.line: The traffic has rendered my punctuality a matter of purely historical interest.
items.right: The traffic has made me late.
wrong: I came early.
The traffic cleared. I got here fast.
I always arrive on time, traffic or not.
items.why: Punctuality is being on time. If yours is only history, you are late.

items.line: I am experiencing a transient deficit of funds until the first of the month.
items.right: I am broke until payday.
wrong: I have lost my bank card.
A friend owes me some money.
My salary was raised.
items.why: Transient means short-lived and a deficit is a shortage: money is briefly missing.

items.line: Kindly refrain from ingesting the final samosa, which I have reserved for my own consumption.
items.right: Hands off the last samosa. It's mine.
wrong: Eat the last samosa. I'm full.
Please save your samosa for later.
The last samosa has gone bad.
items.why: To refrain is to hold yourself back from doing something, and ingesting is eating.

items.line: Your rendition of that song was, shall we say, unencumbered by melody.
items.right: You sang that with no tune at all.
wrong: You sang that very well.
Your song is too long and too heavy.
You forgot the words but kept the tune.
items.why: Unencumbered means not weighed down. A song free of melody has no tune at all.

items.line: The batter's sojourn at the crease proved regrettably brief.
items.right: The batter got out very quickly.
wrong: The batter stayed in for hours.
The batter walked slowly to the crease.
The batter was sorry to be hit.
items.why: A sojourn is a short stay. A regrettably brief stay at the crease means a quick dismissal.

items.line: I implore you to replenish this vessel with the hot brown elixir of my people.
items.right: Please pour me more chai.
wrong: Wash this cup, please.
I beg you to stop making chai.
My ship has sailed away with the tea.
items.why: To implore is to beg, to replenish is to fill up again, and a vessel here is just a cup.

items.line: My mother has expressed a certain scepticism regarding the cleanliness of my room.
items.right: Mum doubts my room is clean.
wrong: Mum cleaned my room herself.
Mum is proud of how clean my room is.
Mum says my room must be repainted.
items.why: Scepticism is doubt. A mother who doubts your room is clean has seen it.

items.line: My preparation for tomorrow's examination may charitably be described as aspirational.
items.right: I have barely studied.
wrong: I have studied very hard.
I hope to teach this exam one day.
I gave money to a charity instead.
items.why: 'Charitably' warns you the truth is worse: aspirational means you only hope to have studied.

items.line: My mobile device has entered a state of terminal energy depletion.
items.right: My phone battery has run out.
wrong: My phone is at the bus terminal.
My phone is charging very fast.
My phone was stolen.
items.why: Terminal here means final, not a bus stand, and depletion means running out.

items.line: I shall be tardy, owing to circumstances entirely of my own negligent making.
items.right: I will be late, and it is my own fault.
wrong: I will be on time this once.
I owe you for making me late.
Someone else has made me late again.
items.why: Tardy means late, and negligent means careless: the speaker is late through carelessness.

items.line: The lecture possessed all the soporific qualities of a warm afternoon after lunch.
items.right: The lecture put me to sleep.
wrong: It was a thrilling talk.
The lecture was held after lunch.
The lecture was warm and friendly.
items.why: Soporific means sleep-inducing, like a warm afternoon.

items.line: Aunty's inquiries into my marital prospects have become somewhat relentless.
items.right: Aunty keeps asking about my marriage.
wrong: Aunty has finally stopped asking.
Aunty has found me a match and everyone is delighted.
Aunty wants to get married again.
items.why: Relentless means not letting up, ever. 'Somewhat' is the speaker being polite.

items.line: The autorickshaw gentleman has declined to proceed in the direction of my desire.
items.right: The auto driver refused to go there.
wrong: The auto driver took a wrong turn.
The driver refused my money.
The driver asked what I desired.
items.why: To decline is to say no. Every commuter in India has met this exact sentence at a street corner.

items.line: Our neighbour's affection for high-volume midnight entertainment is, alas, undiminished.
items.right: The neighbour still plays loud music at night.
wrong: The neighbour has stopped the music.
The neighbour's TV is broken, sadly.
The neighbour is very fond of us, alas.
items.why: Undiminished means not made any smaller. The midnight noise is as strong as ever.

items.line: The heavens have resumed their annual enthusiasm for inundating my commute.
items.right: The rains have flooded my route again.
wrong: The sky is clear and the roads dry.
My commute has got shorter this year.
It only rains once a year on my road.
items.why: To inundate is to flood. Resumed means it has started again, as it does every year.

items.line: The electricity has once more absented itself without prior intimation.
items.right: Another power cut, with no warning.
wrong: The power has come back on early.
The power bill came without any notice.
They warned us about today's power cut.
items.why: Intimation means advance notice, so without intimation means nobody told you first.

items.line: My berth confirmation currently languishes at waiting list number forty-three.
items.right: My train seat is far from confirmed.
wrong: My seat is confirmed in berth 43.
The train is 43 minutes late.
I'll wait for you on platform 43.
items.why: To languish is to be stuck somewhere unpleasant, getting no better.

items.line: Sir, your attempt to circumvent the queue has not gone unobserved.
items.right: Sir, we saw you jump the queue.
wrong: Sir, nobody noticed you skip the queue.
Sir, you walked all the way round the queue.
Sir, you are next in the queue.
items.why: To circumvent is to get round something, and 'not unobserved' is a polite way of saying seen.

items.line: The pressure cooker has emitted its third whistle, heralding the imminent arrival of dal.
items.right: The dal is nearly ready.
wrong: The dal has burnt.
A guard is blowing a whistle at the dal.
The cooker has broken after three whistles.
items.why: To herald is to announce, and imminent means about to happen: the dal is on its way.

items.line: The canine member of our household has, I regret, consumed my assignment.
items.right: My dog ate my homework.
wrong: I chewed my homework with my teeth.
My assignment is about dogs.
My dog is ill. I stayed home.
items.why: Canine means to do with dogs, though canine teeth exist too. Consumed means eaten.

items.line: My sibling has appropriated the remote control and refuses all negotiations.
items.right: My sibling has taken the remote and won't give it up.
wrong: My sibling has returned the remote, feeling sorry.
The remote is quite appropriate for my sibling.
My sibling is ready to talk about sharing the remote.
items.why: To appropriate something is to take it for yourself, often without asking.

items.line: I shall now repair to my chamber for a period of unapologetic slumber.
items.right: I am going for a nap.
wrong: I will mend my bedroom door first.
I am sorry I slept so long.
I can't sleep.
items.why: To repair to a place is simply to go there. It has nothing to do with mending.

items.line: My uncle's relationship with his wallet may best be described as parsimonious.
items.right: My uncle hates spending money.
wrong: My uncle keeps losing his wallet.
My uncle is generous with his money.
My uncle has bought an expensive wallet.
items.why: Parsimonious means unwilling to spend, even when you really could.

items.line: These mangoes, though costing a king's ransom, are conspicuously bereft of flavour.
items.right: These mangoes are costly but tasteless.
wrong: These mangoes are cheap and delicious.
These mangoes were stolen from a king.
These mangoes have too much flavour.
items.why: Bereft means left without. Mangoes bereft of flavour have none.

items.line: I have been reliably informed that you pilfered my charger.
items.right: I hear you stole my charger.
wrong: I hear you fixed my charger.
You told me where my charger was.
I can rely on you for a charger.
items.why: To pilfer is to steal small things, like chargers, pens and the last of the good biscuits.

items.line: Let us not, in the interests of domestic tranquillity, discuss my marks.
items.right: Let's not bring up my marks, to keep the peace.
wrong: Let's discuss my marks. Home is calm.
My marks have brought great peace at home.
I want my marks discussed by all.
items.why: Tranquillity is calm and peace. Talking about these marks would end it at once.

items.line: Your message has been perused and, I fear, summarily disregarded.
items.right: I read your message and ignored it.
wrong: I haven't read your message yet.
I summarised your message for all.
I read it and will reply soon.
items.why: To peruse is to read, and summarily means at once and without fuss: read, then binned.

items.line: I shall be indisposed on Monday, a development I anticipate with some enthusiasm.
items.right: I plan to 'fall ill' on Monday, and I can't wait.
wrong: I am worried I will be ill on Monday.
I will be getting rid of my old things on Monday.
I will be back at my desk, fit and well, on Monday.
items.why: Indisposed is a polite word for unwell. Looking forward to being ill means it is a plan.

items.line: The Wi-Fi's performance has been, to put it generously, intermittent.
items.right: The Wi-Fi keeps cutting out.
wrong: The Wi-Fi is fast all day.
The Wi-Fi was cut off for good.
The Wi-Fi comes free with the room.
items.why: Intermittent means stopping and starting. 'To put it generously' warns it is worse.

items.line: A gentleman from the bank has again telephoned, entirely unsolicited, to offer me a loan.
items.right: A bank agent called again, though I never asked.
wrong: I rang the bank again to ask for a loan.
The bank has solved my loan problem by phone.
A bank agent called to say my loan is cleared.
items.why: Unsolicited means nobody asked for it. Most calls about loans are.

items.line: Your sartorial choices today are nothing if not audacious.
items.right: Your outfit is very bold.
wrong: Your outfit is plain and dull.
Your tailor overcharged you.
Your shoes are new.
items.why: Sartorial means to do with clothes, and 'nothing if not' means above all else.

items.line: It would be remiss of me not to mention that your shoelace has come undone.
items.right: I must tell you: your lace is untied.
wrong: Just so you know: my lace is undone.
I won't mention your shoelace again.
I am sorry I stepped on your lace.
items.why: Remiss means careless about a duty. Here the duty, apparently, is shoelace news.

items.line: Would you be so magnanimous as to relinquish the window seat?
items.right: Could I have the window seat, please?
wrong: Would you like the window seat?
Can you please open the window?
You are a great person for window seats.
items.why: To relinquish is to give something up, and magnanimous means big-hearted. Flattery for a seat.

items.line: I cannot, in good conscience, endorse a dosa this lamentably limp.
items.right: This soggy dosa gets no praise.
wrong: I recommend this dosa to everyone.
This dosa made me cry with joy.
I'm not allowed to eat any dosa.
items.why: To endorse is to publicly approve, and lamentable means so bad it is sad.

items.line: The cat appears to harbour an implacable hostility towards my laptop.
items.right: The cat hates my laptop and cannot be calmed.
wrong: The cat likes to sleep on my laptop.
The cat was cross but has calmed down now.
My laptop has a harbour view for the cat.
items.why: Implacable means impossible to calm down. To harbour a feeling is to keep it inside you.

items.line: My attendance this semester has been, let us agree, largely theoretical.
items.right: I have hardly gone to class.
wrong: I went to every class.
I go only to the theory classes.
My theory marks have improved.
items.why: Something theoretical exists as an idea, not in real life, like this student in class.

items.line: Your excuse possesses all the structural integrity of a wet papad.
items.right: Your excuse falls apart easily.
wrong: Your excuse is honest and solid.
Your excuse has made me hungry.
Your papad got wet in the rain.
items.why: Structural integrity is the strength that holds something up. A wet papad has none.

items.line: I was, at the material time, engaged in the vigorous pursuit of a departing bus.
items.right: I was running after a bus just then.
wrong: I was buying cloth on a bus.
I was stepping off a bus slowly.
I was at my desk when the bus left.
items.why: The material time is the moment that matters, and a departing bus is one that is leaving.

items.line: Permit me to observe that the rice has achieved an unfortunate adhesion to the pan.
items.right: The rice is stuck to the pan.
wrong: The rice came out light and fluffy.
The rice is raw. Cook it more.
The rice must be served at once.
items.why: Adhesion is sticking, as with adhesive tape. Nobody is happy when rice achieves it.

items.line: Your proposed shortcut has, once again, proved spectacularly counterproductive.
items.right: Your shortcut made the trip longer.
wrong: Your shortcut saved us some time.
Your shortcut had great views.
Your shortcut is against the law.
items.why: Counterproductive means it does the opposite of what you wanted, like this shortcut.

items.line: My father holds that twenty-four degrees is the sole acceptable setting for civilised persons.
items.right: Dad insists the AC must stay at 24.
wrong: Dad's shoe soles melt above 24 degrees.
Dad lets everyone pick their own AC setting.
Dad has a college degree from 1924.
items.why: Sole here means only, as in the one and only, and nothing to do with feet or fish.

items.line: Mother has issued a categorical prohibition on further screen time.
items.right: Mum has totally banned the phone.
wrong: Mum asked me to limit my phone use.
Mum has sorted the screens by category.
Mum bought a new phone.
items.why: Categorical means absolute, with no exceptions. A prohibition is a ban.

items.line: In view of your culinary ambitions, I have taken the liberty of ordering food.
items.right: You tried to cook, so I ordered in.
wrong: I love your cooking, so I ordered nothing.
I set you free to order what you like.
Your food tastes great.
items.why: Culinary means to do with cooking. Taking the liberty means doing it without asking.

items.line: I'm afraid the tiffin has been the subject of an unauthorised incursion.
items.right: Someone has raided my lunchbox.
wrong: My tiffin has been shared with permission.
I forgot my tiffin.
My lunchbox is the subject of a class.
items.why: An incursion is a sudden raid into someone else's territory. In this case, the lunchbox.

items.line: This queue appears to be advancing at a glacial pace.
items.right: This queue is moving very slowly.
wrong: This queue is in a very cold place.
This queue is moving very quickly.
This queue has stopped for good.
items.why: Glacial means as slow as a glacier, which is how ice moves. It is not about temperature here.

items.line: His opinions on batting are as copious as his experience of it is negligible.
items.right: He talks a lot about batting but has barely played.
wrong: He has played a lot and says very little about it.
He copies all his batting ideas from others.
He gives batting advice, and it is usually worth hearing.
items.why: Copious means plentiful and negligible means so small it can be ignored. A familiar uncle.

items.line: I am presently disinclined to vacate this bed.
items.right: I don't want to get up.
wrong: I can't get up because I am ill.
I am making this bed right now.
I'm happy to get up now.
items.why: Disinclined means unwilling, and to vacate is to leave. A whole Monday in five words.

items.line: The fact that you have arrived on time is unprecedented, and we are concerned for your health.
items.right: You came on time for once. Are you well?
wrong: You're always on time. We expected it.
You arrived late again and we are annoyed.
You are on time, but your doctor is concerned.
items.why: Unprecedented means it has never happened before, not even once.

items.line: The spice level of this curry exceeds the limits of my constitution.
items.right: This curry is too hot for me.
wrong: This curry is against the law.
This curry needs more chilli.
The salt in this curry is fine.
items.why: Your constitution is your body's strength. Here the word has nothing to do with the law.

items.line: He is a mendacious individual, particularly on the subject of his marks.
items.right: He lies, especially about his marks.
wrong: He is truthful about his marks.
He tops the class in most subjects.
He often mends things for marks.
items.why: Mendacious means lying. It has nothing to do with mending, which he should try instead.

items.line: I had rather hoped for a more felicitous outcome to my driving test.
items.right: My driving test went badly.
wrong: I have passed.
My driving test has been postponed.
My friend Felicity drove me to my test.
items.why: Felicitous means happy or lucky. Hoping for a happier outcome means this one was bad.

items.line: The family group chat has descended into acrimony over seating at lunch.
items.right: The family chat is fighting about lunch seats.
wrong: The family chat agreed happily on lunch seats.
The family is planning a ceremony at lunch.
Nobody in the family group wants any lunch.
items.why: Acrimony means bitter, angry feeling. It is not the same as a ceremony.

items.line: You have, in your own inimitable fashion, locked the keys inside the house.
items.right: Only you could lock the keys inside.
wrong: You are copying how I locked the keys in.
You have had new keys made for everybody.
You left the key with me.
items.why: Inimitable means impossible to copy: so very you that nobody else could manage it.

items.line: I should be most obliged if you would cease humming.
items.right: Please stop humming.
wrong: Thank you for humming so nicely.
I am forced to hum along with you.
Hum it again.
items.why: Obliged here means grateful, not forced, and to cease is to stop.

items.line: An altercation has arisen in the lane concerning the rightful ownership of a parking spot.
items.right: People are arguing in the lane over parking.
wrong: The lane is being altered to add more parking.
A neighbour has kindly offered up a parking spot.
A new parking rule has been put up in the lane.
items.why: An altercation is a loud argument. It is not an alteration, which is a small change.

items.line: Your new ringtone is an affront to the entire compartment.
items.right: Your ringtone is horrible.
wrong: Everyone in front loves your ringtone.
Your ringtone is far too quiet.
Your ringtone is new.
items.why: An affront is an insult. This ringtone has insulted a whole train carriage.

items.line: The canteen's sambar remains stubbornly insipid.
items.right: The sambar still tastes of nothing.
wrong: The sambar is inspiring as always.
The canteen has stopped making sambar.
The sambar is now far too spicy.
items.why: Insipid means flavourless. It looks like inspiring but could hardly be further from it.

items.line: I have resolved to abstain from sweets, beginning immediately after this laddoo.
items.right: I am quitting sweets, right after this one.
wrong: I have quit sweets and won't touch this laddoo.
I will eat sweets only on days with a laddoo.
I will make sweets for everybody tomorrow.
items.why: To abstain is to choose not to have something. As for when, that is always after this one.

items.line: The class monitor has absconded with the attendance register.
items.right: The monitor has run off with the register.
wrong: The monitor is absent today.
The monitor has signed the register.
The monitor has returned the register.
items.why: To abscond is to run away secretly, usually with something you should not have.

items.line: Papa's explanation of the rules proved both interminable and inaccurate.
items.right: Dad's explanation went on forever and was wrong.
wrong: Dad's explanation was short and exactly right.
Dad's explanation finished at the bus terminal.
Dad explained the rules badly, but quickly.
items.why: Interminable means seeming never to end. A terminal is where things stop.

items.line: There is, I regret to report, a dire dearth of milk on the very eve of chai.
items.right: We have run out of milk, just before tea.
wrong: We have far too much milk this evening.
The milk has become very dear this week.
The milk must be boiled before tea.
items.why: A dearth is a shortage of something. Never confuse it with dear, which means costly.

items.line: Allow me to disabuse you of the notion that I shall be washing these dishes.
items.right: I am not washing these dishes.
wrong: I was rude to you about the dishes.
You are quite right, I will wash these.
The dishes are clean.
items.why: To disabuse is to free someone from a wrong belief. It has nothing to do with abuse.

items.line: The clerk at the counter evinced no interest whatsoever in my predicament.
items.right: The clerk cared nothing for my problem.
wrong: The clerk threw me out for my problem.
The clerk gladly sorted out my problem.
The clerk found my plan rather boring.
items.why: To evince is to show clearly, and a predicament is a difficult situation.

items.line: I shall not dignify that remark about my cooking with a response.
items.right: I am too offended to answer that.
wrong: I'll answer your remark politely.
Your remark about my cooking was dignified.
I have already replied to that remark.
items.why: To dignify a remark is to treat it as worthy. Refusing means it was not worth a reply.

items.line: My phone's storage has reached saturation, owing to four thousand photographs of lunch.
items.right: My phone is full of lunch photos.
wrong: Four thousand people liked my lunch photos.
I owe someone for four thousand lunches.
My phone is broken.
items.why: Saturation is being so full that nothing more fits. Owing to simply means because of.

items.line: You appear to be labouring under the misapprehension that this is your chair.
items.right: You think this chair is yours. It isn't.
wrong: You have been working hard on this chair.
You are right. This chair is yours.
You are afraid of this chair for some reason.
items.why: A misapprehension is a wrong belief. Labouring under one means you have not noticed yet.

items.line: Beta, your prolonged silence on the subject of marks is most eloquent.
items.right: Your silence tells me the marks are bad.
wrong: You have explained your marks very well.
You should speak up about your good marks.
Your silence means you have not got your marks.
items.why: Eloquent means speaking clearly and well. A silence can say plenty.

items.line: Aunty, I must decline the fourth helping, as I am entirely replete.
items.right: No more for me, Aunty, I am full.
wrong: Aunty, yes please. One more helping.
Aunty, I must repeat, it is very hot.
Aunty, I helped with the fourth plate.
items.why: Replete means completely full. It is a beautiful word, and it will not work on any aunty.

items.line: The power bank has abdicated its responsibilities.
items.right: The power bank has stopped working.
wrong: A king has given up his power bank.
The power bank now charges twice as fast.
The power bank is with someone responsible.
items.why: To abdicate is to give up a duty or throne. Power banks do it at the worst moment.

items.line: The invigilator prowled among us with an air of baleful omniscience.
items.right: The invigilator seemed menacing and all-knowing.
wrong: The exam supervisor was friendly and relaxed.
The exam supervisor had a sore throat.
The exam supervisor was looking confused and rather lost.
items.why: Baleful means threatening harm. Omniscience is knowing everything, or seeming to.

items.line: Someone has been surreptitiously eating my noodles, and the evidence points to you.
items.right: I think you've been secretly eating my noodles.
wrong: You have shared my noodles with everyone.
I was surprised at how tasty my noodles were.
I can prove that someone ate your noodles.
items.why: Surreptitious means done secretly. Evidence is what gives the secret away.

items.line: I find the prospect of Monday morning singularly unappealing.
items.right: I really don't want Monday to come.
wrong: Only one Monday morning is a problem for me.
I like Monday mornings a great deal.
I find Monday mornings quite amusing.
items.why: Singularly means extremely here, and a prospect is what you see coming. Not just one.

items.line: The bus conductor was, let us say, unreceptive to my proposal of paying tomorrow.
items.right: The conductor wouldn't let me pay tomorrow.
wrong: The conductor happily agreed to let me pay tomorrow.
The conductor did not hear me ask to pay tomorrow.
The bus has no reception for a phone proposal.
items.why: Unreceptive means not willing to listen to or accept an idea.

items.line: Your proposal to split the bill is, I fear, a transparent stratagem to avoid paying for the starters.
items.right: It's a clear trick to skip paying for starters.
wrong: I fear the bill has been split quite fairly.
The bill was printed on clear paper.
You have very kindly offered to pay for all the starters.
items.why: A stratagem is a clever trick, and transparent here means easy to see through.

items.line: My cousin's cricket analysis, though delivered with great fervour, lacks any discernible content.
items.right: My cousin is passionate but says nothing.
wrong: My cousin's cricket talk is full of useful detail.
My cousin has a fever and cannot watch cricket.
My cousin delivers newspapers with cricket scores.
items.why: Fervour is passionate feeling, and discernible means able to be noticed. There is none.

items.line: With the greatest respect, Minister, that is a novel reading of the figures.
items.right: I think you have misread the figures, Minister.
wrong: I respect your reading of the figures.
The figures are from a new book, Minister.
You have read the figures well.
items.why: 'With the greatest respect' nearly always comes before disagreement, and novel here means odd.

items.line: As per my previous email, the attachment was, in fact, attached.
items.right: You didn't read my email. It was attached.
wrong: I forgot the attachment. Here it is.
Please send the attachment with your reply.
My earlier email may not have reached you.
items.why: 'As per my previous email' politely means: I told you already, so read it this time.

items.line: Thank you for your suggestion. We shall certainly take it under advisement.
items.right: We will consider it, and may well do nothing.
wrong: We have accepted your suggestion.
We have asked our lawyers to check it.
We advise you, politely, to withdraw it.
items.why: Under advisement means being thought about. Nothing is promised, and often nothing follows.

items.line: Perhaps we might circle back to your concern once the quarter has closed.
items.right: We will leave your concern for much later.
wrong: We will get back to you about your concern this week.
Your concern will be the reason the quarter closes.
We'll deal with your concern straight away.
items.why: To circle back is to return to something later, which often means putting it off for good.

items.line: The proposal is not without merit, though I would hesitate to fund it.
items.right: It has some good in it, but I would not fund it.
wrong: It has no merit at all, and should be dropped.
It is an excellent proposal, and it deserves full funding.
I am willing to fund it after a short delay.
items.why: 'Not without merit' grants only a little, and hesitate here is a polite way to refuse.

items.line: Going forward, we would encourage you to verify figures before circulating them.
items.right: Your figures were wrong. Check them next time.
wrong: Keep up the good work with the figures.
Your figures were right. Send them out faster.
The team will verify the figures for you.
items.why: 'Going forward' points to the future, but it usually follows a mistake just made.

items.line: Your time management remains a significant opportunity for growth.
items.right: You are bad at managing your time.
wrong: Your time management is growing very fast.
You are in line for a promotion this year.
Your extra time has given you room to grow.
items.why: In a review, 'opportunity for growth' means weakness. The polite word hides the bad news.

items.line: In light of the restructuring, your role has been deemed surplus to requirements.
items.right: You are losing your job.
wrong: Your role is safe.
Your team now needs more people.
You are being paid more than you need.
items.why: Surplus to requirements means more than is needed. Applied to a person, it means let go.

items.line: That is a very interesting idea, and I look forward to hearing the second one.
items.right: That idea is bad. Try another.
wrong: That is a strong idea and I want more like it.
That idea is good. Try it first.
We need at least two ideas to begin.
items.why: In polite English, 'interesting' often means not good, and the 'second one' confirms it.

items.line: That is certainly a brave choice of font for a client presentation.
items.right: That font looks like a mistake.
wrong: That font shows real strength of character.
The client asked for that font specially.
That font is rather hard to read in print.
items.why: When a choice is called brave at work, someone thinks it is a foolish risk.

items.line: Your comments have been duly noted.
items.right: We heard you. Nothing will change.
wrong: We heard you. Changes are coming.
Your comments have made you famous.
We'll reply to your comments next week.
items.why: Duly means properly, and noted means written down. It promises no action at all.

items.line: Your reimbursement remains pending the approval of the competent authority.
items.right: Your refund waits for the right officer to sign.
wrong: A very skilled officer has paid your refund.
Your refund has been rejected by your boss.
Your refund has been approved and is on its way.
items.why: A competent authority is the officer with the power to decide, not a talented one.

items.line: The undersigned begs to state that the aforesaid leave was availed of without prior sanction.
items.right: I took that leave without getting permission.
wrong: My leave was approved well in advance.
I was punished for taking leave earlier.
I'm writing to request that same leave a second time.
items.why: A sanction can be approval or punishment. In an office letter, prior sanction means permission.

items.line: We regret any inconvenience this may have caused.
items.right: Sorry if it bothered you, but we admit nothing.
wrong: We admit, frankly, that this caused you trouble.
We are sorry. We will pay for the trouble.
We expect this to cause you trouble soon.
items.why: 'Any' and 'may have' are hedges: they avoid saying that trouble really happened.

items.line: The committee has, not for the first time, moved the goalposts.
items.right: The committee has changed the rules midway again.
wrong: The committee changed the rules for the first time.
The committee has moved to a new football ground.
The committee has stuck firmly to the agreed rules.
items.why: To move the goalposts is to change the rules after the game has begun.

items.line: The report was quietly kicked into the long grass soon after the election.
items.right: The report was quietly shelved after the vote.
wrong: The report was published after the vote.
The report was thrown out by angry voters.
The report looked at farmland after the vote.
items.why: To kick a matter into the long grass is to delay it until everyone has forgotten it.

items.line: You will be informed of the outcome in due course.
items.right: You'll hear eventually. Don't ask when.
wrong: You'll hear today. Keep your phone on.
The course fee is due on the outcome.
You've already been told the outcome.
items.why: In due course means at some suitable time later. It promises no date at all.

items.line: May I offer some constructive feedback on what you have chosen to call a strategy?
items.right: What you call a strategy isn't really one.
wrong: I admire the strategy you have chosen here.
I would like to help you build a new strategy.
You've chosen a very strong name for it.
items.why: 'What you have chosen to call' means the speaker refuses to agree that it is one.
words: what you have chosen to call

items.line: He has left an impression on the department that will take years to remove.
items.right: He harmed this place for years to come.
wrong: He will be remembered fondly here for years.
He took years to leave the department.
He made a very strong first impression.
items.why: Nobody needs to 'remove' a good impression, so this one was clearly bad.

items.line: She is conscientious to a fault, and the fault is now delaying the project.
items.right: Her excess care is slowing the project.
wrong: She made one error, which delayed the project.
She is careless, and that is delaying the project.
Her good work has saved the project from delay.
items.why: To a fault means too much of a good thing. Here she is too careful.

items.line: Concerns have been raised about the frequency of your absences.
items.right: Someone is unhappy that you miss work so often.
wrong: You have raised concerns about the office.
Your absences have been rising rapidly.
The whole office is worried about your health.
items.why: The passive 'have been raised' hides who complained. Frequency means how often.

items.line: Mistakes were made in the audit, though the memo declines to say by whom.
items.right: The memo admits errors but names nobody.
wrong: The memo blames the auditors by name and demands they resign.
The memo is clear. No errors were made.
The memo says the audit made the errors.
items.why: 'Mistakes were made' admits a fault while hiding who made it. The memo keeps it hidden.

items.line: The management reserves the right to make such changes as it may deem fit.
items.right: We can change anything whenever we like.
wrong: Only fit and healthy staff may ask for changes.
Changes can be made only with staff approval.
The management will make only reasonable changes.
items.why: To deem is to judge or consider. 'As it may deem fit' means whatever it decides.

items.line: The thesis, while ambitious, is innocent of any evidence.
items.right: The thesis aims high but has no evidence.
wrong: The evidence shows that the author is innocent.
The thesis is modest and very well supported.
The thesis is about proving someone not guilty.
items.why: Innocent of means completely without. Here it is a polite way to say no evidence at all.

items.line: The paper would benefit from a clearer sense of why it exists.
items.right: This paper has no clear purpose.
wrong: The paper exists to help people see clearly.
The paper needs a slightly clearer title.
This paper should stay exactly as it is.
items.why: Reviewers say 'would benefit from' when something is missing. Here that is the whole point.

items.line: Some might say the data were selectively presented. I am merely reporting what some might say.
items.right: I suspect the data were cherry-picked, but won't say so.
wrong: Some people are wrong about how the data were shown.
I have checked, and I find the data were presented accurately.
Most people, I find, think the data were random.
items.why: Hiding behind 'some might say' lets a speaker make an accusation without owning it.

items.line: Reasonable people may differ on this, and I am one of them.
items.right: I disagree with you.
wrong: Everyone reasonable agrees with me on this.
People have grown more reasonable over time.
You are right. I am one of them.
items.why: 'Reasonable people may differ' is the polite way of starting to disagree with you.

items.line: Approval is subject to the availability of funds, which are not presently available.
items.right: It's approved only if there's money, and there isn't.
wrong: Funds are available, so it has been approved.
The funds are meant for your subject of study.
It'll be approved, once you've paid a fee.
items.why: 'Subject to' means depending on. Here the thing it depends on does not exist.

items.line: It can hardly be said that the contractor exceeded expectations.
items.right: The contractor did not do well.
wrong: The contractor worked very hard on it.
The contractor did better than expected.
It is forbidden to say anything about it.
items.why: Hardly means almost not. It has nothing to do with working hard.

items.line: The motion was tabled on Friday and will be debated on Monday.
items.right: It was put forward Friday, for debate Monday.
wrong: It was dropped on Friday for good.
It was put aside on Friday, to be forgotten.
The debate was held at a table on Friday.
items.why: In British and Indian usage, to table something is to present it for discussion.

items.line: We shall endeavour to expedite the matter, resources permitting.
items.right: We might hurry this up, if we can manage it.
wrong: This will be done by tomorrow without fail.
We shall put this off, until we have more people.
We'll send a team to inspect the matter.
items.why: To endeavour is to try, to expedite is to speed up, and 'resources permitting' is the escape.

items.line: Whether the budget was adequate is now a moot point, since the project has been cancelled.
items.right: It no longer matters if the budget was enough.
wrong: Everyone must now debate whether the budget was enough.
The budget was large enough.
The budget was too small, so the project was cancelled.
items.why: A moot point once meant one worth debating, but today it usually means one that no longer matters.

items.line: Mr Rao will look after the department pro tem, there being no alternative.
items.right: Mr Rao is in charge for now; there's nobody else.
wrong: Mr Rao is a proven professional for the job.
Mr Rao is the permanent head; it's settled.
Mr Rao was picked from a long list of strong candidates.
items.why: Pro tem is short for pro tempore, Latin for 'for the time being'.

items.line: Decisions here are made on an ad hoc basis, which is to say, by whoever shouts.
items.right: There is no system; the loudest person decides.
wrong: Decisions are made by a special expert panel.
Decisions here are made carefully, after long study.
There is a system; the chair decides.
items.why: Ad hoc means done for one particular purpose, with no general plan behind it.

items.line: The complainant's bona fides have been called into question.
items.right: People now doubt the complainant's honesty.
wrong: Someone has telephoned the complainant.
The complainant's bonus has been questioned.
The complainant has doubted the firm's honesty.
items.why: Bona fides means good faith, which is honesty of intent. To question it is to doubt them.

items.line: The meeting stood adjourned sine die.
items.right: The meeting was put off with no new date.
wrong: The meeting was moved to next Tuesday.
The meeting ended once everyone had signed.
The meeting went on until the end of the day.
items.why: Sine die is Latin for 'without a day'. No new date has been set.

items.line: The committee's findings were discussed in camera.
items.right: The findings were discussed in private.
wrong: The discussion was filmed for the record.
The findings were not discussed.
The findings were discussed with the press.
items.why: In camera is Latin for 'in a chamber': behind closed doors, with no cameras at all.

items.line: Prima facie, the accounts appear to be in order.
items.right: At first look, the accounts seem fine.
wrong: After a full audit, the accounts are proven fine.
On the first page, the accounts look fine.
The accounts, however, are not in the right order.
items.why: Prima facie is Latin for 'at first sight'. It promises no deeper check.

items.line: The report criticises, inter alia, the hostel food.
items.right: The hostel food is one of several things it faults.
wrong: The report criticises the hostel food and nothing else at all.
The report praises the hostel food above all.
The report is mostly about hostel food.
items.why: Inter alia is Latin for 'among other things', so the food is not the only complaint.

items.line: The same rules apply, mutatis mutandis, to part-time staff.
items.right: The same rules apply, adjusted where needed.
wrong: The very same rules apply without any change at all.
Part-time staff, however, are excused.
The rules have been changed to suit full-time staff.
items.why: Mutatis mutandis is Latin for 'with the necessary changes made'. It is not 'exactly the same'.

items.line: The one caveat is that none of this has been tested.
items.right: There's one warning: this is all untested.
wrong: Only one part of this has been tested so far.
There's one warning: only some of it is tested.
We have tested everything thoroughly.
items.why: A caveat is a warning or condition. This one happens to swallow everything before it.

items.line: A cursory glance at the figures would have spared us this meeting.
items.right: Even a quick look would have saved this meeting.
wrong: A long, careful study of the figures was needed.
The figures on screen moved with the cursor.
The meeting gave us a quick look at the figures.
items.why: Cursory means quick and not thorough. Spared us means we need not have met at all.

items.line: The chair offered a perfunctory apology and moved on to lunch.
items.right: The chair's apology was quick and not sincere.
wrong: The chair's apology was long and moving.
The chair refused to apologise to anyone.
The chair apologised perfectly and then ate.
items.why: Perfunctory means done only as a duty, with no real feeling or care.

items.line: It would be disingenuous to call this restructuring anything but a pay cut.
items.right: Honestly, this is just a pay cut.
wrong: It is a clever way of restructuring our pay.
Calling this a pay cut would be dishonest.
This is a restructuring and not a pay cut.
items.why: Disingenuous means not sincere, pretending to know less. It is not the same as ingenious.

items.line: The deliverables remain somewhat nebulous at this juncture.
items.right: Nobody yet knows what we are meant to produce.
wrong: The deliverables have been set out clearly and in full.
The delivery vans are stuck at the junction.
We have already delivered most of the work.
items.why: Nebulous means cloudy and unclear, and a juncture is simply a point in time.

items.line: He has yet to offer a cogent reason for the delay.
items.right: He has given no convincing reason for it.
wrong: He has given many good reasons.
He hasn't yet come to give a reason.
His delay was for an urgent reason.
items.why: Cogent means clear and convincing. It looks like urgent but has a different meaning.

items.line: Pursuant to Clause 9, your deposit stands forfeited.
items.right: Under Clause 9, you lose your deposit.
wrong: Your deposit is safe.
You are chasing us under Clause 9 for your deposit.
Under Clause 9, you keep your deposit a while longer.
items.why: Pursuant to means in accordance with, and forfeited means lost as a penalty.

items.line: Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Company shall bear no liability whatsoever.
items.right: Despite all that, the Company owes you nothing.
wrong: Because of the above, the Company will pay you.
As stated above, the Company stands by all of it.
The Company will pay a limited part of the liability.
items.why: Notwithstanding means in spite of, and the foregoing is whatever was written above it.

items.line: This offer is made without prejudice to our legal position.
items.right: We offer this, but keep all our legal rights.
wrong: This offer is free of bias against anyone.
With this offer, we give up our legal claim.
Our lawyers confirm this offer is legal.
items.why: Without prejudice means making this offer will not harm our legal rights if things go badly.

items.line: We had a robust exchange of views.
items.right: We had a big argument.
wrong: We had a chat.
We agreed on everything.
We swapped very strong opinions on paper.
items.why: Robust here means forceful. Diplomats and managers use it when a meeting turned into a fight.

items.line: The talks were frank and, at moments, cordial.
items.right: The talks were blunt, and only sometimes friendly.
wrong: The talks were honest and warm from start to end.
The talks were polite, but said nothing useful.
The talks were friendly until someone got frank.
items.why: Frank means blunt. 'At moments, cordial' means the friendly parts were rare.

items.line: I don't have the bandwidth to take that on at present.
items.right: I am too busy for that right now.
wrong: My internet is too slow to open that file.
I will take that on after this call.
I have room. I can do that for you.
items.why: Bandwidth is borrowed from the internet. In an office it just means free time and energy.

items.line: Let us pluck the low-hanging fruit before we attempt to boil the ocean.
items.right: Do the easy tasks before any impossible ones.
wrong: Begin with the hardest task and only then take a rest.
Let us hold the office party by the sea.
Do everything at once, however long it takes.
items.why: Low-hanging fruit means easy wins, and boiling the ocean means trying to do far too much.

items.line: Let's take this offline.
items.right: Not here. We'll talk about it later.
wrong: Let's switch off the Wi-Fi.
Print it. We'll read it on paper.
Let's discuss this as a group.
items.why: In meetings, 'take this offline' means stop here and talk privately later. No Wi-Fi involved.

items.line: I have nothing against the idea per se; I merely object to its being carried out.
items.right: I claim to accept the idea but won't let it happen.
wrong: I object to the idea but would let it go ahead.
I am against the idea for one personal reason.
I fully support the idea and I am keen to see it carried out.
items.why: Per se means in itself. Objecting to an idea's being carried out is objecting to the idea.

items.line: The vendor's alleged upgrade has left the system slower than before.
items.right: The vendor claims it upgraded, yet it's slower.
wrong: The vendor's upgrade has made the system quicker.
The vendor, sadly, has been accused of a crime.
The upgrade was real, but the slowness is unrelated.
items.why: Alleged means claimed without proof. The writer is not accepting that any upgrade happened.

items.line: We shall be socialising the decision with stakeholders in the coming weeks.
items.right: The decision is made; we'll just be telling people.
wrong: We will ask everyone's opinion before we decide on this.
We'll throw a party for all the stakeholders.
The decision is open; we'll ask people first.
items.why: To socialise a decision is to spread the news of it. The deciding has already been done.

items.line: Not to put too fine a point on it, the audit found the cupboard bare.
items.right: Bluntly, the audit found no money at all.
wrong: Bluntly, the audit found a few points to fix.
The audit, careful and detailed, found little.
The audit found the cupboards in good order.
items.why: 'Not to put too fine a point on it' means 'to say it bluntly', and a bare cupboard is empty.
words: not to put too fine a point on it

items.line: Your reference states that you are 'always present at your desk'. Nothing else.
items.right: Your old boss found nothing else to praise.
wrong: Your old boss says you are a star employee.
Your old boss says you often work from home.
Your reference was too long to read in full.
items.why: Faint praise damns by leaving out everything that matters. Here only attendance is mentioned.

items.line: That the rival firm also lost money was cold comfort to our shareholders.
items.right: It did little to cheer up our shareholders.
wrong: It made our shareholders feel a great deal better.
Our shareholders wanted the rival firm to lose more.
The shareholders are pleased.
items.why: Cold comfort is a small consolation that does not really help.

items.line: Your degree, impressive though it is, is beside the point.
items.right: Your degree is not relevant here.
wrong: Your degree is the main point here.
Your degree is not so impressive after all.
Your degree was placed beside your papers.
items.why: Beside the point means not connected with what matters. 'Impressive though it is' softens it.

items.line: The seating arrangements left much to be desired.
items.right: The seating arrangements were poor.
wrong: The seating was so good that we wanted more.
We desire many more seats than this.
Many seats were left empty on purpose.
items.why: To leave much to be desired is to fall well short of what you would want.

items.line: Your reply was, to say the least, unhelpful.
items.right: Your reply was extremely unhelpful.
wrong: Your reply was only slightly unhelpful.
Your reply was the shortest of them all.
I can say very little about your reply.
items.why: 'To say the least' means the truth is even stronger than the word chosen.

items.line: Far be it from me to criticise, but who approved this?
items.right: I am criticising this, whoever approved it.
wrong: I would never criticise this, and I approve it.
I live too far away, so I can't judge this.
I'm sure it was approved correctly by someone.
items.why: 'Far be it from me to' usually announces the very thing it claims the speaker will not do.

items.line: The much-advertised product launch proved something of a damp squib.
items.right: The product launch turned out a big letdown.
wrong: The product launch was a runaway success.
The product launch was rained out.
The launch had no advertising at all.
items.why: A squib is a small firework. A damp one fizzles and fails to go off, disappointing everyone.

items.line: The inquiry's report was widely condemned as a whitewash.
items.right: People said the report hid what really happened.
wrong: People, on the whole, praised its honesty.
People said the report was too harsh on the guilty.
People said the building needed fresh white paint.
items.why: A whitewash is a cover-up: painting over faults so that nobody can see them.

items.line: The staffing question, frankly, is a red herring.
items.right: Staffing only distracts from the real issue.
wrong: Staffing is the most urgent issue of all.
Staffing is a dangerous sign of bad trouble.
Staffing has already been sorted out by the new manager.
items.why: A red herring is something that draws attention away from what really matters.

items.line: A three-month delay is, I am told, par for the course.
items.right: Three-month delays are normal here.
wrong: A three-month delay is a rare event here.
The delay is shorter than what we expected.
The delay means that the course costs more.
items.why: Par is the usual score in golf, so par for the course means normal and expected.

items.line: The budget speech turned out to be the minister's swan song.
items.right: It was the minister's last big performance.
wrong: It was the minister's best speech ever.
It was the minister's first major speech.
The minister sang during the speech.
items.why: A swan song is someone's final performance before they leave the stage.

items.line: The outcome of the vote was a foregone conclusion.
items.right: Everyone knew the result before the vote.
wrong: The result of the vote was soon forgotten.
Nobody could have guessed the result of the vote.
The vote, in the end, had no conclusion.
items.why: A foregone conclusion is a result that was certain before it happened.

items.line: Kindly revert at your earliest convenience.
items.right: Please reply as soon as you can.
wrong: Please change it back to the old version.
Please return the item to our office.
Please wait for us to get back to you.
items.why: In Indian office English, revert means reply. Elsewhere it means go back to an earlier state.

items.line: We request you to kindly do the needful at the earliest.
items.right: Please do whatever is required, and soon.
wrong: Please, kindly, be generous to the needy.
Please do it when you have spare time.
We need you in the office early.
items.why: 'Do the needful' is a beloved Indian office phrase meaning do what is necessary.

items.line: Vide your letter under reference, the undersigned regrets inability to process the same.
items.right: About your letter: I am unable to process it.
wrong: I will view your letter and process it later.
I am happy to say your letter has been processed.
About your letter: I regret sending it.
items.why: Vide is Latin for 'see', used in Indian offices to mean 'in reference to'.

items.line: The matter is under active consideration of the Ministry.
items.right: The Ministry has decided nothing so far.
wrong: The Ministry has just approved the matter.
The Ministry has rejected the matter outright.
The Ministry will give its answer tomorrow.
items.why: 'Active consideration' sounds busy but only says it is being thought about, perhaps forever.

items.line: We take exception to the tone of your letter.
items.right: We are offended by how you wrote this.
wrong: We will make an exception for your letter.
We admire the tone of your letter.
Your letter is the only one with this tone.
items.why: To take exception to something is to object to it. It is not the same as making an exception.

items.line: The critic's praise of the novel is not unconvincing, though it is hard to say what exactly is being praised.
items.right: It persuades fairly well, but its target is unclear.
wrong: The praise fails to convince, though its target is clear.
The critic has praised the novel for its clear purpose.
The novel is hard to read, and that is what is praised.
items.why: 'Not unconvincing' is a cautious yes: somewhat convincing, and the rest admits a doubt.

items.line: The reform, ostensibly aimed at the poor, has chiefly enriched those who drafted it.
items.right: Billed as for the poor, it mostly enriched its authors.
wrong: It has helped the poor and has also rewarded its authors well.
It was never aimed at the poor, as its authors admit.
Its authors became poorer while the poor grew rich.
items.why: Ostensibly means apparently but not really: it flags a gap between the claim and the fact.

items.line: Few would now dispute what almost nobody in 1950 was prepared to entertain.
items.right: A view rejected in 1950 is now widely accepted.
wrong: People in 1950 accepted what we now reject.
Few people today accept the view held in 1950.
People in 1950 found this view entertaining.
items.why: 'Few would dispute' means most agree, and to entertain an idea is to be willing to consider it.

items.line: That the treaty failed is beyond doubt; that it was doomed to fail is a comfortable fiction.
items.right: The treaty failed, but failure was not inevitable.
wrong: It failed, and failure was always certain.
We cannot be sure that the treaty failed.
Some say it failed; the author thinks it worked.
items.why: The first clause grants the failure; 'comfortable fiction' rejects the excuse that it had to happen.

items.line: His incredulity is of the convenient kind: it never troubles the beliefs that pay his salary.
items.right: He doubts only what costs him nothing to doubt.
wrong: He questions every belief, including his own.
He is paid to doubt what other people believe.
He doubts his salary and his employer.
items.why: Incredulity means refusal to believe. Calling it convenient says it stops where it would cost him.

items.line: To call the report's conclusions modest is to overstate them.
items.right: Even 'modest' flatters these conclusions.
wrong: The conclusions are bold, and not at all modest.
The conclusions are modest, as they ought to be.
The report has exaggerated its own conclusions.
items.why: Calling them modest would overstate them, so they are even smaller than modest.

items.line: Her claim, though not false, is true only in the sense that a stopped clock is sometimes right.
items.right: Her claim is true only by accident.
wrong: Her claim is completely false.
Her claim is true only on certain days.
Her claim is out of date but was once true.
items.why: A stopped clock is right twice a day by luck. The comparison denies she earned the truth.

items.line: The historian's neutrality is more apparent than real.
items.right: The historian only seems neutral.
wrong: The historian's neutrality is plain for all to see.
The historian is neutral in fact but not in manner.
The historian, being neutral, has no real opinions.
items.why: Apparent here means seeming, not obvious, so 'more apparent than real' means only on the surface.

items.line: If the theory survives, it will be less for its merits than for want of a rival.
items.right: It may last chiefly because it has no competitor.
wrong: If it lasts, it will be for its great merits.
The theory wants a rival in order to survive.
It has rivals, but the most merit of all.
items.why: 'For want of' means for lack of, not out of desire. 'Less for X than for Y' ranks the reasons.

items.line: Nothing in the data precludes the hypothesis, which is all that can be said for it.
items.right: The data merely fail to rule it out.
wrong: The data clearly prove the hypothesis correct.
The data rule out the hypothesis completely.
The data predict the hypothesis in every case.
items.why: To preclude is to rule out. 'All that can be said for it' means it has no other support.

items.line: The minister's remorse lasted precisely as long as the cameras did.
items.right: The minister's regret was only for show.
wrong: The minister regretted it for a very long time.
The minister asked the cameras to leave at once.
The minister felt sorry after the cameras had gone.
items.why: Remorse is deep regret. If it ends when the cameras go, it was never real.

items.line: It is a measure of the book's success that its errors have become the common sense of the field.
items.right: Its success made its errors the accepted view.
wrong: The book has corrected the field's common errors.
The book succeeded because it made no errors.
The field has since corrected the book's errors.
items.why: 'A measure of' shows how great something is. Here the praise carries a sting: the errors spread too.

items.line: Whatever else may be said of the regime, it was not, as its apologists insist, merely misunderstood.
items.right: The author denies it was only misunderstood.
wrong: The author thinks it was merely misunderstood.
Its apologists are sorry for what the regime did.
The author says nothing else can be said of it.
items.why: An apologist defends something; it has nothing to do with saying sorry. The author disagrees.

items.line: The movement's radicalism was largely a matter of vocabulary.
items.right: The movement was radical mostly in what it said.
wrong: The movement changed the language of the nation.
The movement was radical in every possible way.
The movement's actions were extreme; its words were mild.
items.why: 'Largely' limits the claim: most of the radicalism was in the words, not in what was done.

items.line: One need not share the author's despair to admire the precision with which she describes its causes.
items.right: You can admire her analysis without despairing too.
wrong: To admire her analysis, you must share her despair.
Her despair is the only thing worth admiring here.
She describes causes of despair without real precision.
items.why: 'One need not share X to admire Y' separates the two: agreement is not required for respect.

items.line: The assertion that markets correct themselves is, at best, a hope dressed as an observation.
items.right: That claim is a wish pretending to be a fact.
wrong: Markets, it has been observed, correct themselves.
It is the best hope we have for correcting markets.
The claim is true most of the time, but not always.
items.why: 'At best' sets the ceiling: the kindest thing you can call it is a hope, never a finding.

items.line: The film is at its most persuasive when it is least concerned to persuade.
items.right: It convinces best when it isn't trying to convince.
wrong: It convinces best when it is trying hardest to convince.
It never convinces anyone at any point in its length.
It is most persuasive about what concerns it least.
items.why: The 'most' and 'least' are paired to reverse what you expect: the less effort, the more effect.

items.line: Hers is a learning worn so lightly as to be, on occasion, mislaid.
items.right: Her lightly worn learning is sometimes simply lost.
wrong: Her knowledge is heavy and shows in every line.
She studies lightly, yet never gets a single fact wrong.
Her learning is thin, and she always hides that.
items.why: 'Worn lightly' praises unshowy knowledge; 'mislaid' turns it into a gentle jab about her errors.

items.line: The commission's findings, though hedged at every turn, are damning.
items.right: The findings are cautious in wording but severe.
wrong: The findings are so cautious that nobody is blamed.
The findings are bold in wording but mild in effect.
The commission has cleared everyone at each stage.
items.why: Hedged means carefully limited, and damning means showing someone to be guilty. Both are true here.

items.line: Had the author been less enamoured of his paradox, he might have noticed that it was merely a contradiction.
items.right: Too fond of his paradox, he missed the contradiction.
wrong: He noticed the contradiction and so dropped his paradox.
He hated his paradox and so called it a contradiction.
The paradox is brilliant, and he deserves more credit.
items.why: Enamoured means in love with. 'Had he been less' implies he was too much, and so he did not see.

items.line: What passes for consensus in the discipline is often no more than fatigue.
items.right: The field's 'agreement' is often mere exhaustion.
wrong: Scholars in the discipline have reached a true agreement.
Fatigue is the main subject the discipline agrees on.
Experts, it seems, are tired of agreeing.
items.why: 'What passes for' means it only looks like the real thing. Here it is tiredness, not agreement.

items.line: The poet's reputation has suffered less from his detractors than from his admirers.
items.right: His admirers hurt him more than his critics did.
wrong: His critics have done more harm than his fans.
The poet suffered because he had few admirers.
His admirers protected him from his critics.
items.why: Detractors are people who criticise someone. 'Less from X than from Y' means Y did more harm.

items.line: Not all nostalgia is reactionary, but the reactionary is seldom without it.
items.right: Reactionaries are usually nostalgic, but not the reverse.
wrong: All nostalgia is reactionary at heart.
Reactionaries rarely feel any nostalgia about the past at all.
Nostalgia is seldom found among thoughtful people.
items.why: Seldom without means almost always with. Note the direction: the claim does not run both ways.

items.line: It would be uncharitable, though not inaccurate, to describe the policy as an elaborate delay.
items.right: Harsh but true: the policy is a delaying tactic.
wrong: Harsh and false: the policy is no delay.
The policy is a generous charity, the author says.
The policy was delayed by an elaborate process.
items.why: 'Uncharitable, though not inaccurate' concedes the description is unkind and then confirms it.

items.line: The evidence, such as it is, points the other way.
items.right: What little evidence exists goes against this.
wrong: Strong evidence from many good studies points the other way.
There is no evidence either way at all.
The evidence clearly supports this claim.
items.why: 'Such as it is' is a shrug: it admits the evidence is poor even while using it.

items.line: The author concedes the point only to show how little follows from it.
items.right: The author grants it but says it proves little.
wrong: The author grants the point and so changes her whole view.
The author refuses to grant the point at all.
The author says a great deal follows from it.
items.why: To concede is to admit. Conceding 'only to show' means the admission is a setup for a rebuttal.

items.line: Her rejection of empire is unimpeachable; her reasons for it are another matter.
items.right: Her verdict is sound, but her reasoning is doubtful.
wrong: Her reasons are sound; her verdict is doubtful.
She has been impeached for rejecting the empire.
Her verdict and her reasoning are both beyond doubt.
items.why: Unimpeachable means beyond doubt. 'Another matter' is the signal that the reasons are not.

items.line: Such optimism is defensible only if one is careful not to look at the figures.
items.right: The optimism fails once you look at the figures.
wrong: The figures, carefully read, support the optimism.
The optimism can be defended by studying the figures.
The figures are hard to look at, but the view is sound.
items.why: 'Defensible only if' sets a condition, and the condition here is not looking at the evidence.

items.line: Scarcely a chapter passes without a complaint about the very jargon the author goes on to employ.
items.right: The author attacks jargon and then uses it too.
wrong: The author avoids jargon in almost every chapter.
Few chapters contain any complaint about jargon.
The author employs people to remove the jargon.
items.why: 'Scarcely a chapter passes without' means nearly every chapter has it. 'The very' points to the irony.

items.line: It is a book one is glad to have read, which is not the same as enjoying the reading of it.
items.right: It was worth finishing, though not fun to read.
wrong: It was a joy to read from start to finish.
It was not worth reading, and the author knows it.
People were glad when the book went out of print.
items.why: 'Glad to have read' looks back on a finished task. It says nothing about liking the process.

items.line: The theory's elegance has done more to secure its acceptance than its accuracy ever could.
items.right: Beauty won it more followers than accuracy could.
wrong: It was accepted because it was shown to be accurate.
It is elegant, accurate and accepted by everybody.
Its elegance has made it less accepted than accuracy.
items.why: The comparison ranks the causes: elegance did more for its acceptance than truth could have.

items.line: To the extent that the reforms succeeded, they did so despite their architects.
items.right: Any success came in spite of those who planned them.
wrong: The reforms succeeded thanks to the skill of their planners.
The reforms fully succeeded, the planners say.
The architects designed buildings for the reforms.
items.why: 'To the extent that' limits the success, and 'despite their architects' denies the planners any credit.

items.line: Far from undermining his authority, the scandal confirmed what his followers had always wished to believe.
items.right: The scandal strengthened his hold on his followers.
wrong: The scandal destroyed his standing with his followers.
His followers had always wished for a scandal.
His followers began to doubt him after the scandal.
items.why: 'Far from' reverses what you expect: the scandal did the opposite of undermining him.

items.line: There is something faintly comic in a philosopher of freedom who insists on a strict seating plan.
items.right: The writer gently mocks the philosopher's inconsistency.
wrong: The writer praises the philosopher for being so consistent.
The philosopher is famous for his jokes about seating.
The writer thinks that freedom needs strict rules.
items.why: 'Faintly comic' is the stance: a gentle, amused criticism that a free thinker should be so rigid.

items.line: It is not that the argument is wrong; it is that it is not, strictly speaking, an argument.
items.right: It isn't really an argument at all.
wrong: The argument is wrong.
The argument is right but somewhat too strict.
The argument is strict and correct throughout.
items.why: 'It is not that X; it is that Y' swaps one complaint for a stronger one: this is not even an argument.

items.line: The author's modesty, so frequently advertised, is the least convincing thing in the memoir.
items.right: Her constant show of modesty rings false.
wrong: Her modesty is the most convincing part of the book.
The memoir's advertisements are not convincing.
She is truly modest, and rarely mentions it.
items.why: Real modesty is not advertised. Frequently advertised modesty refutes itself.

items.line: Implicit in this celebration of the village is a contempt for those who actually live there.
items.right: Praising the village hides a scorn for its people.
wrong: The writer openly scorns the village and says so.
The villagers celebrate with contempt for others.
The villagers are praised for their simple lives.
items.why: Implicit means present but not said directly, so the scorn is felt under the praise.

items.line: Progress, in this account, is indistinguishable from forgetting.
items.right: As told here, progress is really just forgetting.
wrong: Progress helps us forget the pains of the past.
The author insists all progress is forgetting.
We cannot tell the past from the future.
items.why: 'In this account' limits the claim to one telling of the story, which need not be the truth.

items.line: The regime's critics were, in the official phrase, 'assisting with inquiries'.
items.right: The critics had been detained by the state.
wrong: The critics volunteered to help the inquiry.
The critics were officially cleared by the regime.
The critics had begun their own inquiry.
items.why: 'In the official phrase' warns you of a euphemism: a polite term hiding an unpleasant fact.

items.line: The book's central claim is as unobjectionable as it is uninteresting.
items.right: Nobody could disagree with it, or care.
wrong: The claim is disputed. It is fascinating.
The claim is objectionable and also dull.
The claim is interesting and widely accepted.
items.why: 'As X as it is Y' ties the two: it is so harmless that no one could object and no one would care.

items.line: Whether the author intends the irony is a question the text is careful not to settle.
items.right: The text never shows if the irony is deliberate.
wrong: The text shows clearly that the irony is deliberate.
The author says that there is no irony in the text.
The text is careful to explain the irony to readers.
items.why: To settle a question is to answer it. Here the author leaves it open on purpose.

items.line: Even its critics allow that the treatise is learned, which is the least one might ask of a treatise.
items.right: Its one agreed merit is the least such a book should have.
wrong: Its critics admit that it is the finest treatise of its kind.
Its critics refuse to admit that it is learned at all.
Being learned is the highest praise a treatise can get.
items.why: 'Allow' means grudgingly admit, and 'the least one might ask' makes that one merit a low bar.

items.line: Tolerance, as practised here, amounts to an agreement not to notice.
items.right: Here, tolerance just means looking the other way.
wrong: Tolerance here means truly respecting one another.
This place has made an agreement about its notices.
Tolerance here is practised by everybody, always.
items.why: 'Amounts to' strips something down to what it really is. Here the fine word shrinks to not noticing.

items.line: The chapter on method promises a rigour that the remaining chapters are at pains to avoid.
items.right: The later chapters lack the rigour promised.
wrong: The later chapters are painful and hard to read.
The later chapters work hard to keep up the rigour.
The method chapter avoids rigour; later ones have it.
items.why: 'At pains to' means taking great care to do something. They avoid rigour as if on purpose.

items.line: He writes as though the question had been settled, which is precisely what remains to be shown.
items.right: He assumes the very thing he has yet to prove.
wrong: He has settled the question by clear proof.
He writes only about settled questions.
He admits that nothing remains to be shown.
items.why: 'As though' marks a pretence: he behaves as if it is proved when it is not.

items.line: Her account is persuasive in the way that only an account which omits the inconvenient can be.
items.right: It convinces because it leaves out awkward facts.
wrong: It convinces because it includes every awkward fact.
It is too inconvenient to be at all persuasive.
It omits nothing, though the facts are inconvenient.
items.why: Only an account that omits the awkward facts can persuade like this, so the praise is a charge.

items.line: The party's commitment to reform was, in the end, rhetorical.
items.right: The party backed reform only in words.
wrong: The party asked many questions about reform.
The party carried out reform after much debate.
The party spoke eloquently and reformed the state.
items.why: Rhetorical here means only for show in speech. Note 'in the end': it may have looked real earlier.

items.line: That art should instruct is a doctrine more often preached than practised, and happily so.
items.right: Art rarely teaches, and the writer is glad.
wrong: The writer wishes art would teach more often.
Art teaches often, and the writer is glad about it.
Preachers teach art less often than they should.
items.why: 'More often preached than practised' means rarely done, and 'happily so' shows the writer is pleased.

items.line: Nor is it clear that the poor, in whose name all this is done, were ever consulted.
items.right: It is doubtful anyone ever asked the poor.
wrong: The poor were asked. They wanted this.
The poor were certainly never consulted.
It is clear that the poor were asked many times.
items.why: 'Nor is it clear' raises a doubt, which is weaker than saying they definitely were not asked.

items.line: The scholarship is impeccable; the conclusion, one suspects, preceded it.
items.right: Fine research, but the answer was decided first.
wrong: The research led the writer to the conclusion.
The research is flawed, as is the conclusion.
The research proceeded from a sound conclusion.
items.why: Preceded means came before. 'One suspects' keeps the charge careful while still making it.

items.line: A more generous reader than this one might call the ending ambiguous.
items.right: This reviewer thinks 'ambiguous' is too kind for it.
wrong: The reviewer praises the ending for its ambiguity.
The reviewer expects most readers to be generous.
The reviewer finds the ending quite clear and final.
items.why: 'A more generous reader than this one' distances the reviewer from the kinder word.

items.line: Whatever its merits as history, the film's merits as an alibi are considerable.
items.right: Good history or not, the film works well as an excuse.
wrong: The film's history is considerable and well told.
As history it is strong, but nobody could use it as an excuse.
The film was made by people who had an alibi.
items.why: 'Whatever its merits as X' sets that question aside. An alibi is an excuse for those it serves.

items.line: We are asked to believe, on the strength of a single diary, that the whole court was innocent.
items.right: The writer doubts one diary can clear the whole court.
wrong: The single diary proves the court was innocent.
The writer believes the whole court was innocent.
The diary was written by a very strong believer.
items.why: 'We are asked to believe' signals the writer does not believe it. Single diary shows why.

items.line: Such a view is tenable only by someone who has never had to implement it.
items.right: You can hold that view only if you have not tried it.
wrong: It is easy to put such a view into practice.
Only those who have implemented it hold this view.
Such a view can be held by anyone at all.
items.why: Tenable means able to be defended. 'Only by' limits its defenders to people without experience.

items.line: In attacking the orthodoxy, he has merely substituted his own.
items.right: He has replaced one fixed belief with another.
wrong: He has freed the field from fixed beliefs.
He has defended the old beliefs.
He has bravely attacked his own beliefs.
items.why: Orthodoxy is the accepted belief of a group. 'Merely' shows that changing it achieved little.

items.line: Her defence of the canon would be more persuasive had she read more of it.
items.right: She has not read enough of what she defends.
wrong: She has read the whole canon and defends it well.
Her defence persuades because she is so widely read.
Her defence persuades, though she has read little of it.
items.why: The canon is the group of works seen as the most important. 'Would be, had she' says she has not.

items.line: To say the scheme works because it is effective is merely to beg the question.
items.right: That only assumes what it should be proving.
wrong: That raises an interesting new question.
That is a plea to ask a question.
That proves that the scheme is effective.
items.why: To beg the question is to assume the very thing you are trying to prove. 'Works' equals 'effective'.

items.line: It is hard to overstate the influence of the pamphlet, though many have tried.
items.right: It was hugely influential, yet people still exaggerate it.
wrong: Its influence was quite small, and many overrate it.
Many have tried to write a pamphlet like this one.
Nobody has tried to assess its influence properly.
items.why: 'Hard to overstate' means very great. 'Though many have tried' jokes that people still manage it.

items.line: The hostility that greeted the essay is the best evidence of its accuracy, or so its author would like us to think.
items.right: The author sees proof in the hostility; the writer doubts.
wrong: The critics now admit that the essay was accurate.
The writer agrees; the hostility proves the essay right.
The author was hostile to those who found errors in it.
items.why: 'Or so its author would like us to think' shows the view is the author's, not the writer's.
